notes.front: What is the gross estate, for the federal estate tax (Form 706)?
notes.back: All property in which the decedent had an interest, including property outside the United States, plus certain other items.
notes.explanation: The Form 706 instructions start from everything the decedent had an interest in, wherever it is, then add items such as annuities and some life insurance.
notes.example: Like a full inventory of what someone owned at death, but also counting some things that pass outside the will.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Gross Estate”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The gross estate includes all property in which the decedent had an interest (including property outside the United States).

notes.front: What is the basic exclusion amount (BEA), and what is it for 2025?
notes.back: The basic exclusion amount (BEA) is the inflation-adjusted core of the applicable exclusion amount for gift and estate tax: $13,990,000 for 2025.
notes.explanation: A surviving spouse’s applicable exclusion amount adds any unused exclusion of the last deceased spouse to this basic amount.
notes.example: Like a lifetime allowance for tax-free transfers, but one that shrinks as taxable gifts use it up.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “What’s New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: The applicable exclusion amount consists of the basic exclusion amount ($13,990,000 in 2025) and, in the case of a surviving spouse, any unused exclusion amount of the last deceased spouse (who died after December 31, 2010).

notes.front: What is the unified credit, and what is it called now?
notes.back: The credit applied against gift (and estate) tax on transfers; the Form 709 instructions now call it the applicable credit.
notes.explanation: Form 709 tracks the applicable credit used on gifts in earlier periods, because credit used during life is no longer available later.
notes.example: Like a gift card that pays the tax on transfers, but one card that serves both lifetime gifts and the estate.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Schedule B, Column (c)”, p. 15
notes.evidence: the amount of applicable credit (formerly unified credit) used for gifts made after 1976

notes.front: What is the marital deduction on Form 706?
notes.back: A deduction, listed on Schedule M, for property interests that pass from the decedent to the surviving spouse and are in the gross estate.
notes.explanation: Only interests included in the gross estate can be listed, and nondeductible terminable interests are excluded unless a special election is made.
notes.example: Like a pass-through: what goes to the surviving spouse is deducted now, but it may be taxed when that spouse dies.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Schedule M: Property Interests That You May List”, p. 39
notes.evidence: Generally, you may list on Schedule M (Form 706) all property interests that pass from the decedent to the surviving spouse and are included in the gross estate.

notes.front: What is the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount (DSUE)?
notes.back: The deceased spousal unused exclusion amount (DSUE): the deceased spouse’s exclusion left unused, which the executor may elect to transfer to the surviving spouse.
notes.explanation: A Form 706 filed to transfer it is required regardless of the size of the gross estate.
notes.example: Like unused holiday days that one spouse can pass to the other, but only if the paperwork is filed on time.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Which Estates Must File”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Whose executor elects to transfer the deceased spousal unused exclusion (DSUE) amount to the surviving spouse, regardless of the size of the decedent’s gross estate.

notes.front: What is the portability election?
notes.back: The executor’s election, made on a timely filed Form 706, to transfer the DSUE amount to the surviving spouse.
notes.explanation: Timely means within 9 months of the date of death, or before the end of an extension period if one was granted.
notes.example: Like signing over a leftover allowance to a partner, but valid only if the form reaches the IRS by the deadline.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “When To File: Portability election”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An executor can only elect to transfer the DSUE amount to the surviving spouse if the Form 706 is filed timely, that is, within 9 months of the decedent’s date of death

notes.front: What is the gift tax annual exclusion, and what is it for 2025?
notes.back: The amount of gifts each year to each person that the gift tax excludes: $19,000 for 2025.
notes.explanation: Gifts to someone above this total generally require Form 709; a higher exclusion applies to gifts to a spouse who is not a U.S. citizen.
notes.example: Like a yearly allowance per recipient: stay under it for each person and those gifts need no gift tax return.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “What’s New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: The annual gift exclusion for 2025 is $19,000. See Annual Exclusion, later. For gifts made to spouses who are not U.S. citizens, the annual exclusion has increased to $190,000.

notes.front: What is gift-splitting?
notes.back: An election by married donors to treat all gifts either spouse makes to third parties as made one-half by each spouse.
notes.explanation: The consenting spouse agrees in a signed Notice of Consent, so a gift by one spouse can use both spouses’ exclusions.
notes.example: Like two people splitting a restaurant bill evenly, even though only one of them handed over the card.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Part III, Line 7. Consent of Spouse”, p. 8
notes.evidence: consent to treat all gifts made to third parties as having been made one-half by each spouse

notes.front: What is the generation-skipping transfer tax (GST tax), and who is a skip person?
notes.back: The generation-skipping transfer tax (GST tax) applies to transfers to skip persons: donees two or more generations below the donor, such as grandchildren.
notes.explanation: It is reported with the gift tax on Form 709; the instructions assign each donee a generation to test whether the donee is a skip person.
notes.example: Like a toll on money that jumps over the children’s generation, charged on top of any gift tax.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Gifts Subject to Both Gift and GST Taxes”, p. 10
notes.evidence: is a skip person if that donee is assigned to a generation that is two or more generations below the generation assignment of the donor.

notes.front: What is the Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR), and where is it filed?
notes.back: The Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR), FinCEN Form 114, is filed with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, not the IRS.
notes.explanation: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network is a Treasury bureau separate from the IRS, so the FBAR does not go with the tax return, unlike Form 8938.
notes.example: Like a declaration about foreign accounts, but sent to a financial-crimes office instead of the tax office.
introduces: Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Introduction”
notes.evidence: Unlike Form 8938, the FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) is not filed with the IRS. It must be filed directly with the office of Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), a bureau of the Department of the Treasury, separate from the IRS.
uses: Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts

notes.front: What is a specified foreign financial asset, reported on Form 8938?
notes.back: A financial account at a foreign financial institution, or certain foreign investment assets held outside a financial account, such as foreign stock.
notes.explanation: The Form 8938 instructions list both kinds, the second only if held for investment and not in an account at a financial institution.
notes.example: Like a list of foreign savings and investments, but excluding things such as foreign real estate held directly.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Types of Specified Foreign Financial Assets”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Specified foreign financial assets include the following assets. 1. Financial accounts maintained by a foreign financial institution. 2. The following foreign financial assets if they are held for investment and not held in an account maintained by a financial institution.

notes.front: What is the foreign earned income exclusion (FEIE), and on which form is it figured?
notes.back: The foreign earned income exclusion (FEIE) lets a qualifying person exclude foreign earned income from income; it is figured on Form 2555.
notes.explanation: Form 2555 also figures the housing exclusion or deduction, and you cannot exclude or deduct more than your foreign earned income for the year.
notes.example: Like a tax-free allowance for pay earned abroad, but only for people who pass the residence or presence tests.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2555 (2025), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: If you qualify, you can use Form 2555 to figure your foreign earned income exclusion and your housing exclusion or deduction. You cannot exclude or deduct more than the amount of your foreign earned income for the year.

notes.front: What is the bona fide residence test for the FEIE?
notes.back: Being a bona fide resident of a foreign country or countries for an uninterrupted period that includes an entire tax year.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two tests, alongside physical presence; your tax home must also be in the foreign country throughout the period.
notes.example: Like settling in abroad for good, but the residence must span at least one whole tax year.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Frequently Asked Questions: Foreign Earned Income”, p. 36
notes.evidence: foreign country or countries for an uninterrupted period that includes an entire tax year, or you must be physically present in a foreign country or countries for at least 330 full days during any period of 12 consecutive months.

notes.front: What is the physical presence test for the FEIE?
notes.back: Being physically present in a foreign country or countries for 330 full days during a period of 12 consecutive months.
notes.explanation: Pub 54 bases the test only on how long you stay abroad, not on your intentions or the kind of residence you set up.
notes.example: Like counting nights abroad on a calendar, whatever the reason for the stay.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Requirements”, p. 18
notes.evidence: a foreign country (or countries) for 330 full days during a period of 12 consecutive months. The 330 days don’t have to be consecutive.

notes.front: Walt, a U.S. citizen, dies owning a flat in Spain and an annuity. Are they in his gross estate?
notes.back: Yes, both: the gross estate covers property outside the United States and also includes annuities.
notes.choices:
A) Neither: foreign property and annuities are outside it
B) The flat only
C) Both the flat and the annuity
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the Form 706 instructions include property outside the United States and name annuities among the extra items.
notes.explanation: The gross estate starts with all property the decedent had an interest in, wherever it is, and its open list of additions names annuities, some lifetime transfers and joint estates with right of survivorship.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Gross Estate”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The gross estate includes all property in which the decedent had an interest (including property outside the United States). It also includes: • Certain transfers made during the decedent’s life without an adequate and full consideration in money or money’s worth, • Annuities,

notes.front: For a citizen or resident who died in 2025, when must a Form 706 be filed? Name both situations.
notes.back: When gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and specific exemption is over $13,990,000; or when the executor elects to transfer the DSUE amount.
notes.explanation: The threshold matches the 2025 basic exclusion amount, and the DSUE route applies regardless of the size of the gross estate.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Which Estates Must File”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Whose gross estate, plus adjusted taxable gifts and specific exemption, is more than $13,990,000; or

notes.front: Carl, a U.S. citizen, died in 2025 with a gross estate of $9,000,000. He had made $5,500,000 of adjusted taxable gifts and used no specific exemption. Must his executor file Form 706?
notes.choices:
A) No: the gross estate alone is under $13,990,000
B) Yes: the total with adjusted taxable gifts is over $13,990,000
C) No: lifetime gifts are reported only on Form 709
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the filing test adds adjusted taxable gifts to the gross estate before comparing with $13,990,000.
notes.explanation: Lifetime taxable gifts count towards the filing threshold, so a gross estate below the basic exclusion amount can still require a return.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Which Estates Must File”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Whose gross estate, plus adjusted taxable gifts and specific exemption, is more than $13,990,000; or

notes.front: An executor can elect to transfer the DSUE amount only if Form 706 is filed timely: within {{c1::9 months}} of the date of death, or within an extension.
notes.back: 9 months.
notes.explanation: Portability is an election, and the Form 706 instructions make it depend on a timely return; a late return loses it unless specific relief applies.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “When To File: Portability election”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An executor can only elect to transfer the DSUE amount to the surviving spouse if the Form 706 is filed timely, that is, within 9 months of the decedent’s date of death

notes.front: How is the DSUE amount figured?
notes.back: The lesser of the basic exclusion amount at the decedent’s death, or the decedent’s applicable exclusion amount less the Part II, line 5 figure.
notes.explanation: The amount must be figured on the deceased spouse’s estate tax return, which is why a return is needed to pass it on.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Part VI, Section C: DSUE amount”, p. 21
notes.evidence: The DSUE amount is the lesser of (a) the basic exclusion amount in effect on the date of death of the decedent whose DSUE is being figured, or (b) the decedent’s applicable exclusion amount less the amount on Part II, line 5 on the Form 706

notes.front: Hana dies in 2025 with a $2,000,000 estate, well under the filing threshold. Her husband wants her unused exclusion. What must her executor do?
notes.back: File Form 706 on time and elect portability, transferring her DSUE amount to him.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the DSUE passes automatically
B) File a timely Form 706 and elect portability
C) Nothing can be done: small estates cannot transfer DSUE
notes.choicesExplained: A: portability is an election made on Form 706. C: the return is required when the executor elects portability, regardless of the size of the gross estate.
notes.explanation: An estate below the threshold has no filing requirement of its own, but the DSUE transfer needs a Form 706 whatever the size of the gross estate.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Which Estates Must File”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Whose executor elects to transfer the deceased spousal unused exclusion (DSUE) amount to the surviving spouse, regardless of the size of the decedent’s gross estate.

notes.front: When is Form 706 due, and how is more time to file requested?
notes.back: Within 9 months after the date of death; Form 4768 requests an automatic 6-month extension to file.
notes.explanation: The instructions tie the deadline to the date of death, not to a calendar date, and give Form 4768 as the extension route.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “When To File”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You must file Form 706 to report estate and/or GST tax within 9 months after the date of the decedent’s death.

notes.front: Rita died on 10 March 2025. When is her estate’s Form 706 due, and until when with an automatic extension?
notes.back: Due 10 December 2025; with the 6-month extension, 10 June 2026.
notes.choices:
A) 15 April 2026, like an income tax return
B) 10 December 2025; 10 June 2026 if extended
C) 10 March 2026; 10 September 2026 if extended
notes.choicesExplained: A: Form 706 runs from the date of death, not April 15. C: the period is 9 months, not 12.
notes.explanation: 10 March 2025 + 9 months = 10 December 2025; + 6 more months = 10 June 2026.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “When To File”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Use Form 4768, Application for Extension of Time To File a Return and/or Pay U.S. Estate (and Generation-Skipping Transfer) Taxes, to apply for an automatic 6-month extension of time to file.

notes.front: On Schedule E (Form 706), when is a joint interest a qualified joint interest?
notes.back: When decedent and surviving spouse held it as tenants by the entirety, or as the only joint tenants with right of survivorship.
notes.explanation: Qualified joint interests go in Part I of Schedule E; all other joint interests go in Part II.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Schedule E, Part I. Qualified joint interests”, p. 29
notes.evidence: a joint interest is a qualified joint interest if the decedent and the surviving spouse held the interest as: • Tenants by the entirety, or • Joint tenants with right of survivorship if the decedent and the decedent’s spouse are the only joint tenants.

notes.front: Can the special section 2040(b) treatment apply to property held jointly with a surviving spouse who is not a U.S. citizen?
notes.back: No. Such joint interests go in Part II of Schedule E, not Part I.
notes.explanation: The instructions deny the spousal joint-interest treatment in that case and send the property to the general part of the schedule.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Schedule E, Part I”, p. 29
notes.evidence: You cannot claim the special treatment under section 2040(b) for property held jointly by a decedent and a surviving spouse who is not a U.S. citizen.

notes.front: Two brothers owned a cabin as joint tenants with right of survivorship. One dies. Which part of Schedule E (Form 706) reports the cabin?
notes.back: Part II: it is not a qualified joint interest, because the joint tenants were not spouses.
notes.choices:
A) Part I, as a qualified joint interest
B) Part II, with all other joint interests
C) Neither: survivorship property is outside the gross estate
notes.choicesExplained: A: qualified joint interests need the decedent and spouse as the only joint tenants, or a tenancy by the entirety. C: the includible portion of such joint estates is in the gross estate.
notes.explanation: A qualified joint interest is a spousal holding, so a joint tenancy between brothers falls into the general category.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Schedule E, Part I and Part II”, p. 29
notes.evidence: Joint interests that do not meet either of the two requirements above should be entered in Part II.

notes.front: When is the marital deduction allowed for property passing to a surviving spouse who is not a U.S. citizen?
notes.back: Only if it passes in a qualified domestic trust, or is transferred or irrevocably assigned to one before the estate return is filed.
notes.explanation: A qualified domestic trust keeps the marital deduction but defers the tax: estate tax is imposed under section 2056A as distributions are made from the trust.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Schedule M: Qualified Domestic Trust”, p. 42
notes.evidence: The marital deduction is allowed for transfers to a surviving spouse who is not a U.S. citizen only if the property passes to the surviving spouse in a QDOT or if such property is transferred or irrevocably assigned to a QDOT before the decedent’s estate tax return is filed.

notes.front: May nondeductible terminable interests be listed on Schedule M for the marital deduction?
notes.back: No, unless the executor is making the qualified terminable interest property election for them.
notes.explanation: The general rule lets property passing to the surviving spouse be listed, but terminable interests are carved out unless that election is made.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Schedule M: Property Interests That You May List”, p. 39
notes.evidence: However, do not list any Nondeductible terminable interests (described later) on Schedule M (Form 706) unless you are making a QTIP election.

notes.front: Omar dies leaving his house outright to his wife, a U.S. citizen. The house is in his gross estate. Where does it appear for the marital deduction?
notes.back: On Schedule M (Form 706), as a property interest passing to the surviving spouse.
notes.choices:
A) On Schedule M, for the marital deduction
B) Nowhere: property left to a spouse is outside the gross estate
C) Only on the wife’s own Form 709
notes.choicesExplained: B: the house is included in the gross estate first, then deducted. C: a bequest at death is an estate matter, not a gift she reports.
notes.explanation: An outright bequest to a citizen spouse of property included in the gross estate is what Schedule M lists.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Schedule M: Property Interests That You May List”, p. 39
notes.evidence: Generally, you may list on Schedule M (Form 706) all property interests that pass from the decedent to the surviving spouse and are included in the gross estate.

notes.front: When is life insurance on the decedent, payable to someone other than the estate, included on Schedule D (Form 706)?
notes.back: When the decedent held any incident of ownership in the policy at death.
notes.explanation: Proceeds payable to the estate are included in full; proceeds payable to others are included when the decedent kept ownership rights, alone or with others.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 706 (Rev. September 2025), “Schedule D: Insurance Payable to Beneficiaries Other Than the Estate”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Include on Schedule D (Form 706) the proceeds of all insurance on the life of the decedent not receivable by, or for the benefit of, the decedent’s estate if the decedent possessed at death any of the following incidents of ownership

notes.front: When must a domestic estate file Form 1041?
notes.back: When it has gross income of $600 or more in a tax year.
notes.explanation: Form 1041 reports the estate’s own income after death, separately from the estate tax on Form 706.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Income Tax Return of an Estate: Filing Requirements”, p. 22
notes.evidence: Every domestic estate with gross income of $600 or more during a tax year must file a Form 1041.

notes.front: Must a domestic estate file Form 1041 if a beneficiary is a nonresident alien, whatever its gross income?
notes.back: Yes. The personal representative must file regardless of the estate’s gross income.
notes.explanation: Pub 559 makes a nonresident alien beneficiary an exception to the income test.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Income Tax Return of an Estate: Filing Requirements”, p. 22
notes.evidence: If one or more of the beneficiaries of the domestic estate are nonresident aliens, the personal representative must file Form 1041, regardless of the estate’s gross income.

notes.front: A domestic estate earns $450 of interest in its tax year. All beneficiaries are U.S. citizens. Must it file Form 1041?
notes.back: No: $450 is under the $600 gross income threshold, and no beneficiary is a nonresident alien.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, every estate files Form 1041
B) No, its gross income is under $600
C) Yes, because interest is always reported on Form 1041
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the filing test is gross income of $600 or more, unless a beneficiary is a nonresident alien.
notes.explanation: $450 is $150 below $600, and the nonresident alien exception does not apply.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Income Tax Return of an Estate: Filing Requirements”, p. 22
notes.evidence: Every domestic estate with gross income of $600 or more during a tax year must file a Form 1041.

notes.front: Can a gift of a future interest use the annual exclusion?
notes.back: No. Only present interests, where the donee has immediate rights to use, possess and enjoy the property or its income, qualify.
notes.explanation: The Form 709 instructions draw the line by whether the donee’s rights begin now or only at some future date.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Annual Exclusion”, p. 4
notes.evidence: A gift of a future interest cannot be excluded under the annual exclusion. A gift is considered a present interest if the donee has all immediate rights to the use, possession, and enjoyment of the property or income from the property.

notes.front: In 2025 an aunt puts $10,000 in trust for her niece, who can use it only from age 30. Must the aunt file Form 709?
notes.back: Yes. A future interest gets no annual exclusion, so Form 709 is required even though the gift is under $19,000.
notes.choices:
A) No: the gift is under $19,000
B) Yes: a future interest is not covered by the annual exclusion
C) No: gifts in trust are never reported
notes.choicesExplained: A: the $19,000 exclusion covers present interests only. C: gifts in trust are reported on Form 709 like other gifts.
notes.explanation: The niece has no immediate right to use the money, so the gift is a future interest and the whole $10,000 counts.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Who Must File”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Certain gifts, called future interests, are not subject to the $19,000 annual exclusion and you must file Form 709 even if the gift was under $19,000.

notes.front: When must a U.S. citizen or resident generally file Form 709 for 2025 gifts to someone other than a spouse?
notes.back: When gifts to that person total more than $19,000 in 2025.
notes.explanation: The return is required whether or not any tax is ultimately due; certain transfers and gifts to a spouse follow separate rules.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Who Must File”, p. 2
notes.evidence: If you gave gifts to someone in 2025 totaling more than $19,000 (other than to your spouse), you must generally file Form 709.

notes.front: Nora, unmarried, gives her nephew $25,000 in cash in 2025 and makes no other gifts. Must she file Form 709, and does she necessarily owe gift tax?
notes.back: She must file, as the gift is over $19,000; tax may still be zero, since a return is required whether or not tax is due.
notes.choices:
A) No return: no tax will be due
B) Return required; tax is not necessarily due
C) Return required and tax is due on $25,000
notes.choicesExplained: A: the return is required whether or not any tax is ultimately due. C: the first $19,000 is excluded, and credit may cover the rest.
notes.explanation: $25,000 − $19,000 annual exclusion = $6,000 of taxable gift, which must be reported even if no tax results.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Who Must File”, p. 2
notes.evidence: you must file a gift tax return (whether or not any tax is ultimately due) in the following situations. • If you gave gifts to someone in 2025 totaling more than $19,000 (other than to your spouse), you must generally file Form 709.

notes.front: When is Form 709 generally filed?
notes.back: Between January 1 and April 15 of the year after the gift; the next business day if April 15 is a weekend or holiday.
notes.explanation: Form 709 is an annual return, so it covers the calendar year of the gift.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “When To File”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Generally, you must file Form 709 no earlier than January 1, but not later than April 15, of the year after the gift was made.

notes.front: Leo makes a reportable gift on 20 December 2025. What is the window for filing his Form 709 (no extension)?
notes.back: From 1 January 2026 to 15 April 2026.
notes.choices:
A) By 31 December 2025
B) From 1 January 2026 to 15 April 2026
C) Within 9 months of the gift
notes.choicesExplained: A: Form 709 cannot be filed before January 1 of the following year. C: 9 months is the Form 706 period after a death.
notes.explanation: The gift year is 2025, so the return is due in the following year: not before 1 January 2026 and not after 15 April 2026.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “When To File”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Generally, you must file Form 709 no earlier than January 1, but not later than April 15, of the year after the gift was made.

notes.front: What are two conditions spouses must meet to split gifts?
notes.back: Any two, among others: married to each other at the gift; no remarriage that year if later divorced or widowed; neither a nonresident non-citizen.
notes.explanation: The Form 709 instructions list all the conditions that must apply, including one about powers of appointment.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Part III—Spouse’s Consent on Gifts to Third Parties”, p. 7
notes.evidence: You and your spouse were married to one another at the time of the gift. • If divorced or widowed after the gift, you did not remarry during the rest of the calendar year. • Neither of you was a nonresident not a citizen of the United States at the time of the gift.

notes.front: Once spouses elect gift-splitting for a year, which gifts are split, and who is liable for each spouse’s gift tax?
notes.back: All gifts to third parties made while married that year; the liability for each spouse’s entire gift tax becomes joint and several.
notes.explanation: The election is all or nothing for the year, and consenting makes each spouse answerable for the other’s gift tax.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Part III—Spouse’s Consent on Gifts to Third Parties”, p. 8
notes.evidence: parties during the calendar year (while you were married) must be split. If the consent is effective, the liability for the entire gift tax of each spouse is joint and several.

notes.front: How does the consenting spouse agree to gift-splitting on the current Form 709?
notes.back: By signing a Notice of Consent attached to the donor’s return; the consenting spouse no longer signs the return itself.
notes.explanation: The spousal consent lines moved to a new Part III of Form 709, with the signed notice attached.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “What’s New: Part III”, p. 2
notes.evidence: A consenting spouse is no longer required to sign the return but must sign a Notice of Consent to be attached to the donor’s return.

notes.front: In 2025 only Raj makes gifts: $30,000 cash to his niece, a present interest. His wife consents to split. Must both spouses file Form 709?
notes.back: No. Only Raj must file: only one spouse gave, the gift to the niece is not over $38,000, and it is a present interest.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: both always file when gifts are split
B) No: only Raj files, under Exception 1
C) No one files: split gifts are never reported
notes.choicesExplained: A: both generally file, but Exception 1 lets only one file here. C: a gift tax return is required to split gifts, whatever their amount.
notes.explanation: Split, the gift is $15,000 from each spouse, within each $19,000 exclusion. All three Exception 1 conditions hold, so only one return is needed.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Exception 1”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Exception 1. During the calendar year: • Only one spouse made any gifts, • The total value of these gifts to each third-party donee does not exceed $38,000, and • All of the gifts were of present interests.

notes.front: Only the donor spouse must file Form 709 for a split-gift year. Where does the consenting spouse’s Notice of Consent go?
notes.back: One Notice of Consent, attached to the donor spouse’s return.
notes.choices:
A) Attached to the donor spouse’s return
B) Filed separately with the consenting spouse’s Form 1040
C) Nowhere: consent is implied by marriage
notes.choicesExplained: B: the notice goes with the gift tax return, not an income tax return. C: the election is valid only with a signed Notice of Consent.
notes.explanation: When only one spouse must file, only one notice is needed, and it travels with that spouse’s Form 709.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Part III, Line 7. Consent of Spouse”, p. 8
notes.evidence: If only one spouse is required to file a gift tax return, then only one Notice of Consent is required, and it must be attached to the donor spouse’s return.

notes.front: The basic credit amount for 2025 is {{c1::$5,541,800}}.
notes.explanation: This credit is the tax counterpart of the $13,990,000 basic exclusion amount; the table of basic exclusion and credit amounts pairs the two.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “What’s New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: The basic credit amount for 2025 is $5,541,800. See Table of Basic Exclusion and Credit Amounts.

notes.front: A client says: “I can give away only $5,541,800 in my lifetime before gift tax.” Using 2025 figures, what is wrong?
notes.back: $5,541,800 is the basic credit amount, a tax figure; the basic exclusion amount, $13,990,000, is the transfer figure.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: $5,541,800 is the exclusion
B) $5,541,800 is the credit; the exclusion is $13,990,000
C) There is no lifetime figure, only the annual exclusion
notes.choicesExplained: A: the instructions call $5,541,800 the basic credit amount. C: the applicable exclusion amount is a lifetime figure alongside the annual exclusion.
notes.explanation: The credit offsets tax, so it is smaller than the amount of transfers it covers; the instructions give both figures separately.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “What’s New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: The basic credit amount for 2025 is $5,541,800. See Table of Basic Exclusion and Credit Amounts. The applicable exclusion amount consists of the basic exclusion amount ($13,990,000 in 2025)

notes.front: Which lifetime transfers carry GST tax reported on Form 709 as direct skips?
notes.back: Transfers during the donor’s life that are subject to the gift tax, of an interest in property, and made to a skip person.
notes.explanation: All three features must be present; a transfer is subject to the gift tax if it must be reported on Schedule A of Form 709.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Transfers Subject to the GST Tax”, p. 4
notes.evidence: An inter vivos direct skip is a transfer made during the donor’s lifetime that is: • Subject to the gift tax, • Of an interest in property, and • Made to a skip person.

notes.front: Every donor has a lifetime exemption from the GST tax; for 2025 it is {{c1::$13,990,000}}.
notes.explanation: It equals the 2025 basic exclusion amount; the instructions note it was $1 million for transfers made through 1998.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Schedule D, Part 2—GST Exemption Reconciliation”, p. 21
notes.evidence: Every donor is allowed a lifetime GST exemption. The amount of the exemption for 2025 is $13,990,000.

notes.front: Which donee is a skip person for the GST tax: the donor’s daughter or the donor’s granddaughter?
notes.back: The granddaughter: she is two generations below the donor.
notes.choices:
A) The daughter
B) The granddaughter
C) Both
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: a daughter is one generation below the donor, and a skip person must be two or more generations below.
notes.explanation: Generation assignment decides it: one generation down is not enough, two is.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 709 (2025), “Gifts Subject to Both Gift and GST Taxes”, p. 10
notes.evidence: is a skip person if that donee is assigned to a generation that is two or more generations below the generation assignment of the donor.

notes.front: What is the FBAR reporting threshold?
notes.back: Foreign financial accounts whose aggregate value exceeds $10,000 at any time during the calendar year.
notes.explanation: The value is cumulative across accounts, so several small accounts can together cross the line.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Reporting threshold”
notes.evidence: Aggregate value of financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any time during the calendar year.

notes.front: Ella, a U.S. citizen, has two foreign bank accounts. On one day in 2025 they held $6,000 and $5,000. Must she file an FBAR, and for which accounts?
notes.back: Yes, for both: together they held $11,000, more than $10,000, at one time.
notes.choices:
A) No: neither account exceeded $10,000
B) Yes, but only for the larger account
C) Yes, for both accounts
notes.choicesExplained: A: the test is the combined balance. B: once the aggregate is over $10,000, both accounts are reported.
notes.explanation: $6,000 + $5,000 = $11,000, which is over $10,000 on that day.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Reporting threshold”
notes.evidence: This is a cumulative balance, meaning if you have 2 accounts with a combined account balance greater than $10,000 at any one time, both accounts would have to be reported.

notes.front: A foreign account over which you have only signature authority: is it reportable on Form 8938, on the FBAR, or both?
notes.back: FBAR: yes, subject to exceptions. Form 8938: no, unless you otherwise have an interest in the account.
notes.explanation: The FBAR reaches accounts you can control, while Form 8938 turns on having an interest in the asset.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Types of foreign assets and whether they are reportable”
notes.evidence: Foreign financial account for which you have signature authority No, unless you otherwise have an interest in the account as described above Yes, subject to exceptions

notes.front: Dev must file an FBAR for calendar year 2025 and cannot finish by the April date. What is the deadline, and must he request more time?
notes.back: Received by 15 April 2026, with an automatic 6-month extension to 15 October 2026; no request is needed.
notes.choices:
A) 15 April 2026, with an automatic extension to 15 October 2026
B) 15 April 2026, with no extension possible
C) With his tax return, extended only by Form 4868
notes.choicesExplained: B: the FBAR has an automatic 6-month extension. C: the FBAR is not filed with a federal tax return.
notes.explanation: The comparison page gives an April 15 due date with an automatic extension to October 15, and the FBAR is filed separately from the return.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “When do you have to file?”
notes.evidence: Received by April 15 (6-month automatic extension to Oct 15)

notes.front: Who must file Form 8938?
notes.back: A specified person with an interest in specified foreign financial assets worth more than the applicable reporting threshold, unless an exception applies.
notes.explanation: The comparison page adds that Form 8938 is filed with the income tax return, and the assets must be reported even if none affects the tax.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Who Must File”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Unless an exception applies, you must file Form 8938 if you are a specified person (see Specified Person, later) that has an interest in specified foreign financial assets and the value of those assets is more than the applicable reporting threshold.

notes.front: For an unmarried taxpayer living in the United States, what is the Form 8938 reporting threshold?
notes.back: Specified foreign financial assets over $50,000 on the last day of the tax year or over $75,000 at any time during it.
notes.explanation: The same figures apply to a married person filing separately; higher thresholds apply to joint filers and to those living abroad.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Reporting Thresholds: Unmarried taxpayers”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If you are not married, you satisfy the reporting threshold only if the total value of your specified foreign financial assets is more than $50,000 on the last day of the tax year or more than $75,000 at any time during the tax year.

notes.front: For a married couple living in the United States and filing jointly, what is the Form 8938 reporting threshold?
notes.back: Specified foreign financial assets over $100,000 on the last day of the tax year or over $150,000 at any time during it.
notes.explanation: The joint figures are double the unmarried ones.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Reporting Thresholds: Married taxpayers filing a joint income tax return”, p. 4
notes.evidence: you satisfy the reporting threshold only if the total value of your specified foreign financial assets is more than $100,000 on the last day of the tax year or more than $150,000 at any time

notes.front: Sofia, single and living in Ohio, holds foreign stock outside any account. It peaked at $70,000 in 2025 and was worth $60,000 on 31 December. Must she file Form 8938?
notes.back: Yes: $60,000 on the last day of the year is over $50,000, even though the $70,000 peak is not over $75,000.
notes.choices:
A) No: her peak value never exceeded $75,000
B) Yes: her year-end value exceeded $50,000
C) No: stock is not a specified foreign financial asset
notes.choicesExplained: A: meeting either test is enough. C: foreign stock held for investment outside a financial account is a specified foreign financial asset.
notes.explanation: Year-end test: $60,000 > $50,000, met. Any-time test: $70,000 is not over $75,000. One test met means she files.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Reporting Thresholds: Unmarried taxpayers”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If you are not married, you satisfy the reporting threshold only if the total value of your specified foreign financial assets is more than $50,000 on the last day of the tax year or more than $75,000 at any time during the tax year.

notes.front: A married couple in Texas files jointly. Their specified foreign financial assets peaked at $120,000 in 2025 and were $90,000 at year end. Must they file Form 8938?
notes.back: No: $90,000 is not over $100,000 at year end, and $120,000 is not over $150,000 at any time.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: $120,000 is over $100,000
B) No: neither joint threshold is exceeded
C) Yes: the unmarried $75,000 test applies to each spouse
notes.choicesExplained: A: $100,000 is the year-end test; the any-time test is $150,000. C: joint filers use the joint thresholds.
notes.explanation: Year-end: $90,000 ≤ $100,000. Any time: $120,000 ≤ $150,000. Neither test is met.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Reporting Thresholds: Married taxpayers filing a joint income tax return”, p. 4
notes.evidence: you satisfy the reporting threshold only if the total value of your specified foreign financial assets is more than $100,000 on the last day of the tax year or more than $150,000 at any time

notes.front: Foreign stock not held in a financial account, and foreign partnership interests: reportable on Form 8938, on the FBAR, or both?
notes.back: Form 8938 only. Neither is reported on the FBAR.
notes.explanation: The FBAR covers financial accounts, while Form 8938 also covers foreign investment assets held outside an account.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Types of foreign assets and whether they are reportable”
notes.evidence: Foreign stock or securities not held in a financial account Yes No Foreign partnership interests Yes No

notes.front: A U.S. citizen owns a flat in Lisbon directly, in her own name. Is it reportable on Form 8938 or the FBAR?
notes.back: Neither: foreign real estate held directly is not reportable on either form.
notes.choices:
A) Form 8938 only
B) FBAR only
C) Neither form
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the comparison table marks foreign real estate held directly “No” for both forms.
notes.explanation: Real estate is not a financial account and, held directly, not a specified foreign financial asset.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Types of foreign assets and whether they are reportable”
notes.evidence: Foreign real estate held directly No No

notes.front: What civil penalty applies for failing to file Form 8938?
notes.back: Up to $10,000, plus $10,000 for each 30 days of non-filing after IRS notice, to a maximum of $60,000; criminal penalties may apply.
notes.explanation: The extra amounts build up only after the IRS has sent notice of the failure to disclose.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Penalties”
notes.evidence: Up to $10,000 for failure to disclose and an additional $10,000 for each 30 days of non-filing after IRS notice of a failure to disclose, for a potential maximum penalty of $60,000; criminal penalties may also apply

notes.front: For FBAR civil penalties assessed before 1 August 2016, what were the non-willful and willful maximums?
notes.back: Non-willful: up to $10,000. Willful: up to the greater of $100,000 or 50% of account balances.
notes.explanation: The comparison page adds that FBAR civil penalties are now adjusted each year for inflation, and criminal penalties may also apply.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Penalties”
notes.evidence: Civil monetary penalties are adjusted annually for inflation. For civil penalty assessment prior to Aug 1, 2016, if non-willful, up to $10,000; if willful, up to the greater of $100,000 or 50 percent of account balances; criminal penalties may also apply

notes.front: If you fail to file a required Form 8938, how long can the statute of limitations for that year stay open?
notes.back: For all or part of the return, until 3 years after the date you file Form 8938.
notes.explanation: The clock does not start on the missing information until the form arrives.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Statute of Limitations”, p. 11
notes.evidence: If you fail to file Form 8938 or fail to report a specified foreign financial asset that you are required to report, the statute of limitations for the tax year may remain open for all or a part of your income tax return until 3 years after the date on which you file Form 8938.

notes.front: You omit more than $5,000 of income relating to specified foreign financial assets. How long can the IRS assess tax for that year?
notes.back: At any time within 6 years after you filed your return.
notes.explanation: The Form 8938 instructions extend the assessment period for this kind of omission beyond the usual one.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Extended Statute of Limitations for Failure To Include Income”, p. 11
notes.evidence: If you do not include in your gross income an amount relating to one or more specified foreign financial assets, and the amount you omit is more than $5,000, any tax you owe for the tax year can be assessed at any time within 6 years after you filed your return.

notes.front: After an IRS notice, a client keeps failing to file a required Form 8938 for many months. What is the potential maximum civil penalty for that failure to disclose?
notes.choicesExplained: A: $10,000 is only the initial penalty before continued non-filing after notice. C: the comparison page caps the potential maximum at $60,000.
notes.explanation: $10,000 initial penalty + $10,000 for each 30 days after notice, with the total capped at $60,000; criminal penalties are separate.
notes.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements, “Penalties”
notes.evidence: Up to $10,000 for failure to disclose and an additional $10,000 for each 30 days of non-filing after IRS notice of a failure to disclose, for a potential maximum penalty of $60,000

notes.front: Arun filed his 2025 return on 1 June 2026, under an extension, but left out $8,000 of interest from a foreign account. Until when can the IRS assess the tax?
notes.back: Until 1 June 2032: 6 years after he filed, because the omission is over $5,000.
notes.choices:
A) 1 June 2029, 3 years after filing
B) 1 June 2032, 6 years after filing
C) At any time: there is no limit
notes.choicesExplained: A: the usual 3-year period becomes 6 years when omitted foreign-asset income is over $5,000. C: there is no limit only for a fraudulent return or no return.
notes.explanation: $8,000 > $5,000, so the 6-year rule applies: 1 June 2026 + 6 years = 1 June 2032. A return filed early would count from the due date instead.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8938 (Rev. November 2021), “Extended Statute of Limitations for Failure To Include Income”, p. 11
notes.evidence: If you do not include in your gross income an amount relating to one or more specified foreign financial assets, and the amount you omit is more than $5,000, any tax you owe for the tax year can be assessed at any time within 6 years after you filed your return.

notes.front: Which form do certain U.S. officers, directors or shareholders of certain foreign corporations file?
notes.back: Form 5471, Information Return of U.S. Persons With Respect To Certain Foreign Corporations.
notes.explanation: Pub 54 lists it among forms filed with Form 1040, for each applicable foreign corporation.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Forms That Must Be Filed With the IRS With Form 1040”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Certain U.S. persons who are officers, directors, or shareholders in certain foreign corporations must file Form 5471

notes.front: Which form reports a U.S. person’s dealings with certain foreign partnerships?
notes.back: Form 8865, Return of U.S. Persons With Respect to Certain Foreign Partnerships.
notes.explanation: It covers reporting on controlled foreign partnerships and transfers to foreign partnerships, among other things.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Forms That Must Be Filed With the IRS With Form 1040”, p. 12
notes.evidence: A U.S. person must file Form 8865, Return of U.S. Persons With Respect to Certain Foreign Partnerships

notes.front: Which form reports transactions with foreign trusts and receipt of certain large foreign gifts or bequests?
notes.back: Form 3520, filed separately from Form 1040.
notes.explanation: Pub 54 places Form 3520 among the forms filed separately, unlike Forms 5471 and 8865, which go with Form 1040.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Forms That Must Be Filed With the IRS Separately From Form 1040”, p. 13
notes.evidence: U.S. persons (and executors of estates of U.S. decedents) file Form 3520, Annual Return To Report Transactions With Foreign Trusts and Receipt of Certain Foreign Gifts

notes.front: Nadia, a U.S. citizen, inherits $150,000 from her aunt, a foreign individual. Which information return may she have to file?
notes.back: Form 3520, Part IV: a bequest from a foreign individual totalling more than $100,000.
notes.choices:
A) Form 3520
B) Form 5471
C) Form 8865
notes.choicesExplained: B: Form 5471 concerns foreign corporations. C: Form 8865 concerns foreign partnerships.
notes.explanation: $150,000 is over the $100,000 figure for gifts or bequests from a foreign individual or foreign estate.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Gifts and bequests”, p. 93
notes.evidence: You may have to report information on your gifts or bequests on Form 3520, Part IV, if you received: 1. A gift or bequest from a foreign individual or foreign estate

notes.front: For 2025, the maximum foreign earned income exclusion is {{c1::$130,000}}.
notes.explanation: The maximum is adjusted each year; the Form 2555 instructions report the increase for 2025.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2555 (2025), “What’s New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: For 2025, the maximum exclusion amount has increased to $130,000.

notes.front: Which two things must both be true to qualify for the FEIE?
notes.back: You meet the tax home test, and you meet either the bona fide residence test or the physical presence test.
notes.explanation: The tax home must be in a foreign country throughout the period of residence or presence that you rely on.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2555 (2025), “Who Qualifies”, p. 1
notes.evidence: You may qualify for the foreign earned income exclusion and the housing exclusion or deduction if both of the following apply. • You meet the tax home test (discussed later). • You meet either the bona fide residence test or the physical presence test (discussed later).

notes.front: Marco qualifies for the FEIE for all of 2025 and earns $150,000 of foreign wages. Ignoring housing, how much of it can he exclude?
notes.back: $130,000; the remaining $20,000 stays taxable.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the exclusion is capped at the 2025 maximum. C: $120,000 is not the 2025 maximum.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2555 (2025), “What’s New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: For 2025, the maximum exclusion amount has increased to $130,000.

notes.front: Under the physical presence test, must the 330 full days abroad be consecutive?
notes.back: No. They must fall within a period of 12 consecutive months, but need not be consecutive.
notes.explanation: Pub 54 bases the test only on the length of stay, so trips home break the run of days but not the count.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Requirements”, p. 18
notes.evidence: The 330 days don’t have to be consecutive. The physical presence test is based only on how long you stay in a foreign country or countries.

notes.front: Which test can a resident alien use for the FEIE: physical presence, bona fide residence, or both?
notes.back: Physical presence always; bona fide residence only if a citizen or national of a country with a United States income tax treaty.
notes.explanation: U.S. citizens may use either test; Pub 54 limits the residence test for resident aliens to treaty-country nationals.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Frequently Asked Questions: Foreign Earned Income”, p. 36
notes.evidence: U.S. citizens may qualify under either test. The physical presence test applies to all resident aliens, while the bona fide residence test applies to resident aliens who are citizens or nationals of a country with which the United States has an income tax treaty in effect.

notes.front: Over 12 consecutive months, Jin spent 340 full days in Singapore, broken by a 3-week trip home in the middle. Does he meet the physical presence test?
notes.back: Yes: 340 full days in the 12 months is at least 330, and the days need not be consecutive.
notes.choices:
A) No: the trip home broke the period
B) Yes: 340 full days abroad within 12 months
C) No: he must also intend to stay abroad
notes.choicesExplained: A: the 330 days don’t have to be consecutive. C: the test does not depend on your intentions.
notes.explanation: 340 ≥ 330 within one 12-month window; the trip home only removes days from the count.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Requirements”, p. 18
notes.evidence: This test doesn’t depend on the kind of residence you establish, your intentions about returning, or the nature and purpose of your

notes.front: Clara, a U.S. citizen and calendar-year filer, became a bona fide resident of Germany on 1 July 2024 and still lives there. What is the first full tax year her residence period includes?
notes.back: 2025: her uninterrupted residence first includes an entire tax year once 1 January to 31 December 2025 is covered.
notes.choicesExplained: A: she was resident for only half of 2024. C: 2025 already falls entirely within her residence.
notes.explanation: The bona fide residence period must include a whole tax year; from 1 July 2024 onwards, the first whole calendar year inside it is 2025.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Frequently Asked Questions: Foreign Earned Income”, p. 36
notes.evidence: foreign country or countries for an uninterrupted period that includes an entire tax year

notes.front: Bona fide residence test or physical presence test: what does each measure?
notes.back: Bona fide residence: being a resident abroad for a period including a whole tax year. Physical presence: 330 full days abroad in 12 months.
notes.explanation: Physical presence counts only days, ignoring intentions and the kind of residence; bona fide residence looks at the residence itself.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Requirements”, p. 18
notes.evidence: The physical presence test is based only on how long you stay in a foreign country or countries. This test doesn’t depend on the kind of residence you establish, your intentions about returning, or the nature and purpose of your
